strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: extending SAM3's Promptable Concept Segmentation to full instruction-following segmentation (PIS) is a natural and relevant step, and the paper articulates the weakness of the agentic SAM3+MLLM pipeline (information loss from collapsing instructions to NPs, multi-pass overhead) convincingly.

Sensible and clearly described technical design: the hierarchical S-Adapter/C-Adapter cascade, mask distribution alignment (KL) loss, and uncertainty-aware hard-region supervision are well-motivated, and the frozen-backbone design directly addresses the stated goal of preserving SAM3's concept grounding.

Ablation studies (Table 2) are internally consistent and support each design choice: removing curriculum stages, alignment loss, or hard-region supervision each degrades performance in plausible and explained ways.

The scalable data engine (MLLM annotation, agentic verification, human-in-the-loop correction) is a useful engineering contribution, and the paper is refreshingly honest about limitations (single-instance bias, preliminary status, future work).

Quantitative results (Table 1) show SAM3-I outperforming SAM3+Agent baselines on both simple and complex instructions with fewer parameters and single-pass inference, while preserving concept-level performance.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly self-describes as preliminary: a footnote states 'Preliminary results. Comprehensive evaluation is ongoing,' and Sec. 6 calls the work 'an initial feasibility study.' This substantially weakens the case that the central claims are established rather than suggestive.

Evaluation relies on a single benchmark (PACO-LVIS-Instruct) that the authors constructed themselves using the same MLLM-based generation pipeline used to build the training data. This creates circularity and risks linguistic and distributional bias; there is no evaluation on established external referring/reasoning segmentation benchmarks (e.g., RefCOCO/+/g, ReasonSeg), which are mentioned only as future work.

Baselines are limited to SAM3 and SAM3+Agent variants. No comparison against existing referring expression segmentation or instruction-grounding models (e.g., LISA, GLaMM, or similar MLLM-based segmenters), making it hard to judge where SAM3-I stands relative to the broader state of the art.

Reproducibility is currently weak: the code availability statement is a placeholder ('The source code is available here' with no actual URL), the data engine's system prompts, few-shot examples, human-correction protocol details, and annotation quality statistics are not provided, and the *-marked concept-level scores (retained from naive SAM3) blur what SAM3-I itself contributes at the concept level.

The instruction taxonomy (concept/simple/complex) and dataset statistics are given, but no analysis of instruction diversity, verifier accuracy, inter-annotator agreement, or measurement of how hard the generated 'complex reasoning' instructions actually are, leaving dataset quality claims under-evidenced.

Although framed as a language-centric contribution relevant to ACL (instruction understanding, referring expressions), the linguistic analysis is thin; the paper does not characterize failure modes by instruction type beyond aggregate metrics.

strengths: The problem is well-motivated and timely: SAM3's restriction to short noun-phrase prompts is a genuine limitation, and unifying concept-level (PCS) and instruction-level segmentation within the SAM family is a sensible research direction with clear practical relevance to referring/reasoning segmentation.
The three-level instruction taxonomy (concept / simple / complex) is clearly articulated and gives the work a coherent conceptual framing.

The data construction pipeline is described in reasonable detail (MLLM annotation, agentic inspection, human-in-the-loop correction) and yields a sizable resource (843K instruction–mask pairs), which could be of independent value to the community.

The ablation study (Table 2) supports the claimed contributions of the staged curriculum, the distribution alignment loss, and the uncertainty-aware hard-region supervision, with consistent trends across simple and complex instructions.
The paper is candid about its scope, explicitly labeling results as a preliminary feasibility study and discussing limitations such as N-to-1 instance bias and the lack of broader evaluations.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity is the most serious concern: the benchmark (PACO-LVIS-Instruct) is generated by the authors' own pipeline, training and test instructions come from the same distribution and the same generator (Qwen3-VL), and the only comparison is against SAM3 or SAM3 plus an agent built from the very model family used to create the data. There is no evaluation on any established external benchmark (e.g., RefCOCO/+/g, ReasonSeg, refClef), so the reported gains cannot be interpreted as general instruction-following ability.

The claim of preserving SAM3's concept-level capability is not empirically supported: Table 1 marks the concept-level scores of SAM3-I with '*' and the caption admits these are simply 'naive SAM3's concept-level scores' copied over, not re-measured. The central 'without sacrificing original capabilities' claim is therefore assumed rather than evidenced.

The paper self-identifies as incomplete ('Preliminary results. Comprehensive evaluation is ongoing'), which undermines its readiness for archival publication; results are single-run with no variance, seeds, or significance testing.

The agent baseline appears weak and possibly under-tuned: SAM3+Agent with Qwen3-VL-8B is limited to 3 iterative rounds, and the improvement of SAM3-I over it on complex instructions is modest (51.0 vs 48.2 gIoU), leaving the efficiency-vs-quality trade-off less decisive than claimed.

The data quality control has a self-verification circularity: the annotator and inspector are instances of the same MLLM (Qwen3-VL-8B), and the 100%-accuracy acceptance rule likely biases the corpus toward instructions that are easy for that model, i.e., precisely the ones SAM3-I is then evaluated on. No human audit statistics, inter-annotator agreement, or estimated corpus error rate are reported.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the source-code link is a placeholder ('available here'), and key details are missing (adapter dimensions and parameter counts, training schedule, learning rates, how negative instructions are actually used in training, exact prompt templates for generation and inspection).

Technical novelty is limited: bottleneck adapters, a two-stage curriculum, KL-based prediction alignment, and disagreement-weighted losses are all standard components; the contribution is primarily an integration/system paper, which would need stronger empirical evidence to justify the framing of a new paradigm ('Promptable Instruction Segmentation').

The reported gIoU metric is non-standard ('average of all per-image IoU'), making numbers difficult to compare against the referring-segmentation literature; standard cIoU/oIoU reporting would be expected.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: extending SAM3's Promptable Concept Segmentation to full natural-language instructions (Promptable Instruction Segmentation), removing the costly MLLM-agent rewrite/filter loop while keeping concept grounding.

Sensible and parameter-efficient technical design: frozen SAM3 backbone with a cascaded S-Adapter/C-Adapter hierarchy, distribution-alignment (KL) and uncertainty-weighted hard-region losses, and a staged curriculum that mirrors the instruction taxonomy.

A structured, three-level instruction taxonomy (concept / simple / complex) and a documented semi-automatic data engine (MLLM annotation, agentic verification with negative distractors, human correction) that yields a large instruction-mask corpus (45K images, 843K instructions).
Quantitative gains over SAM3+Agent baselines (e.g., +12.4 gIoU on simple, +2.8 on complex) with a smaller parameter count and single-pass inference, plus ablations supporting each design component.
Notably honest framing: the authors explicitly label the work an initial feasibility study, discuss N-to-1 instance bias, and outline scaling/architecture/evaluation limitations.
weaknesses: The experimental section carries a footnote stating 'Preliminary results. Comprehensive evaluation is ongoing,' which is a serious completeness concern for a submission; the paper is not a finished evaluation of its own claims.

Evaluation is confined to the authors' self-constructed PACO-LVIS-Instruct benchmark. There is no evaluation on any established referring or reasoning segmentation benchmark (e.g., RefCOCO/+/g, gRefCOCO, ReasonSeg), so results cannot be compared against the existing referring-segmentation literature, and generalization is untested.

Potential circularity in data construction: the same MLLM family (Qwen3-VL-8B) is used to generate, verify, and effectively define the training/test instructions, so the benchmark may reflect that model's linguistic distribution; no human evaluation of instruction quality or statistics on inter-annotator agreement in Stage 3 are reported.

The concept-level scores for SAM3-I are marked with an asterisk indicating the authors 'retain naive SAM3's concept-level scores' rather than re-measuring them on their pipeline; presenting copied numbers alongside new ones weakens the claim that capabilities are preserved.

Reproducibility is asserted (code 'available here', promised dataset release) but unverifiable from the manuscript; key details such as adapter placement granularity, exact training schedules, and how test instructions were quality-controlled are underspecified.

Fit to ACL is marginal: the contribution is vision-centric (segmentation architecture and data engine), with natural language serving mainly as the interface; the linguistic analysis is shallow (average 15.3 words) and there is no NLP-grounded analysis of instruction understanding.

Minor presentation issues: an unbound 'SAM-I' typo, a placeholder hyperlink for code, and a Table 1 baseline configuration (2B agent) that is substantially weaker than the 8B agent actually shown in qualitative comparisons.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: extending SAM3 from short-NP concept prompts to free-form instruction following (Promptable Instruction Segmentation) is a natural and practically relevant next step for the SAM family, and the agent-free single-pass design addresses real limitations of the SAM3+MLLM pipeline.

The cascaded S-/C-Adapter design with staged curriculum is well motivated by the instruction hierarchy, and the ablation suite is unusually thorough: multi-stage vs. single-stage, cascaded vs. single adapter, each alignment loss individually, and hyperparameter sensitivity for ρ and m, with results that consistently support the design choices.

HMPL-Instruct is a substantial resource: 849K instructions over 44K images spanning concept/simple/complex levels, object/part granularity, and one-to-one/one-to-many/one-to-all cardinalities; the human-in-the-loop construction pipeline and the dual-panel annotation tool for one-to-many subset grounding are described in actionable detail (Appendix B), and dataset statistics are clearly benchmarked against prior work in Table 1.

Strong empirical results: large gains over SAM3 Agent and competitive performance on external benchmarks (RefCOCO, Ref-ZOM), which partially mitigates the concern of evaluating only on a self-built test set.
Good reproducibility posture: implementation details (adapter dimensions, trainable parameter count, hyperparameters, hardware) are provided, and code plus dataset are claimed to be released.
weaknesses: Evaluation fairness is unclear on the main benchmark (Table 3/8): it is not stated whether LISA and UniPixel were trained or fine-tuned on HMPL-Instruct. Since HMPL-Instruct is derived from PACO-LVIS and the test split follows PACO-LVIS, the very low baseline scores (e.g., LISA at ~20-30 gIoU) may reflect distribution mismatch rather than inferior capability, making the headline comparisons hard to interpret.

The claim that SAM3-I 'preserves SAM3's strong concept recall ability' is not actually measured: Table 2 marks concept-level scores with '*' indicating they 'retain naive SAM3's concept-level scores' rather than evaluating SAM3-I on concept prompts. Freezing the backbone does not guarantee no interference from adapter/detector-side adapters, so this central claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

Potential train/test circularity: the primary quantitative evidence is on the authors' own test set built from the same source images and generated with MLLMs whose style may match the annotator model used in training; external validation (RefCOCO, Ref-ZOM) helps but is limited to two benchmarks and one-to-one settings.

The one-to-many setting, which the paper highlights as a key differentiator, is very small (2,941 samples, 7,449 masks), so the strong claims about subset-level reasoning rest on limited data; the paper does not report per-setting sample sizes for the test split.
Ablations evaluate each alignment loss individually but never report combined-loss-minus-one results; whether the four losses are complementary or redundant when jointly applied is not shown.

Several clarity/quality issues: the code/dataset URL is missing ('available at to'), abstract lacks the link, typos ('SAM-I', 'perform well to diverse', 'fifth raw'), and negative instructions are generated but their use in training or evaluation is never specified.

No runs with variance or significance tests are reported, and there is no discussion of how gIoU on a mixture of granularities compares to prior reporting conventions, which complicates cross-paper comparison.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated task: extending SAM3's promptable concept segmentation to free-form natural-language instructions is a natural and relevant direction for the community, and the proposed Promptable Instruction Segmentation (PIS) formulation with a three-level instruction hierarchy (concept / simple / complex) is clearly articulated.

HMPL-Instruct is a substantial resource: ~850K instructions over 44K images with object- and part-level annotations and diverse instruction-instance cardinalities (one-to-one, one-to-many, one-to-all), built via a documented multi-stage pipeline combining MLLM annotation, agentic verification, and human correction (with a detailed annotation tool description in the appendix).

The technical design is reasonable and parameter-efficient: frozen SAM3 backbone with cascaded S-/C-Adapters and four alignment losses (contrastive, parent-rank anchoring, mask KL, uncertainty-weighted hard-region supervision), each individually motivated.
The ablation study is unusually thorough: staged training vs. single-stage, cascaded vs. single adapter, each loss ablated separately, and hyperparameter sensitivity (ρ, m) analyzed in the appendix.
Evaluation spans the authors' benchmark plus external ones (RefCOCO, Ref-ZOM), and qualitative examples illustrate genuine instance-level discrimination beyond category-level grounding.
Ethical and artifact statements are provided; the dataset construction is documented in enough detail to support future reuse.
weaknesses: Evaluation fairness is the decisive weakness: on the main benchmark (HMPL-Instruct, Tables 2 and 3), the baselines (LISA, UniPixel, SAM3 Agent) were evidently not trained on this dataset, while SAM3-I was. The large margins (+22 to +31 gIoU) therefore conflate architectural benefit with training-data access. No baseline is fine-tuned on HMPL-Instruct, so the central claim that SAM3-I's design (rather than simply the new training data) drives the gains is not established. Notably, on the external RefCOCO benchmark where the comparison is fairer, SAM3-I (76.3 gIoU) actually loses to UniPixel (78.1).

The claim that SAM3-I 'preserves' concept-level performance is not empirically verified: Table 2 simply re-reports SAM3's original scores marked with an asterisk, even though adapters are inserted into the detector and could alter outputs. A measured concept-level evaluation after adaptation is needed.

The dataset is derived solely from PACO-LVIS, and the example instructions in Fig. 7 follow highly formulaic templates ('Identify the ... that ...', 'Locate the two ... used for ...'), raising concerns about linguistic diversity and possible annotation shortcuts that favor the proposed model; evaluation is also confined to a single test distribution defined by the authors.
No code or dataset link is provided at review time ('available at' is blank in the manuscript), so reproducibility cannot be verified; this is a stated requirement for Findings-level soundness.

Novelty is moderate: cascaded bottleneck adapters for frozen foundation models and contrastive/ranking/KL alignment losses are established techniques; the primary novelty is their combination and the new task formulation, which is closer to an engineering extension of SAM3 than a conceptual advance.

The main text lacks statistical rigor: results appear to be single-run numbers with no variance or significance reporting, and some numbers are difficult to cross-check (e.g., Table 2 simple-instruction 59.7 gIoU vs. Table 3 one-to-one 60.8, one-to-all 60.9 — the aggregate is below all components).

Hierarchical instruction levels (simple vs. complex) are defined and labeled by the authors' own pipeline; no external validation of this taxonomy or of annotation consistency (e.g., inter-annotator agreement) is reported.
Writing contains several unsubstantiated or overstated claims ('first of its kind in the SAM family', 'appealing performance' repeatedly) that a careful revision should temper.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and timely gap: extending SAM3's promptable concept segmentation to free-form natural-language instructions (Promptable Instruction Segmentation), unifying concept-level and instruction-level grounding in a single-pass model rather than an external MLLM agent loop. The motivation is well argued with concrete examples.

The proposed method is technically coherent: instruction-aware cascaded adapters (S-Adapter for simple referring, C-Adapter for complex NP-free instructions), combined with four complementary alignment losses (instruction contrastive, parent-rank concept anchoring, mask KL alignment, uncertainty-weighted hard-region supervision) and a three-stage training curriculum, with the SAM3 backbone frozen to preserve concept recall.

The HMPL-Instruct dataset is a substantive contribution: 850K instructions over 44K images with a three-level instruction hierarchy, object- and part-level granularity, and one-to-one/one-to-many/one-to-all cardinalities. The human-in-the-loop construction pipeline (automatic generation, agentic verification, human correction, dedicated annotation tool for one-to-many) is described in detail, including an interface appendix and annotation protocol.

Experiments are reasonably broad: comparisons against SAM3, a Qwen3-VL-8B agent variant, LISA, ReLA, and UniPixel on HMPL-Instruct, RefCOCO, and Ref-ZOM; ablations cover each loss, the cascaded vs. single adapter, and staged vs. single-stage training, plus hyperparameter sensitivity for rho and m in the appendix.

The claims of preserving SAM3's concept-level ability are supported by design (frozen backbone) and by reported numbers, and the qualitative results illustrate genuine instance discrimination and reasoning beyond category-level bias.
Reproducibility is aided by released code and dataset, implementation details (adapter dimensions, hyperparameters, hardware), and an artifact/ethics statement.
weaknesses: Primary evaluation is on the authors' own benchmark (HMPL-Instruct), where their model was trained; other methods (LISA, UniPixel, SAM3 Agent) do not appear to be trained on HMPL-Instruct, making the large margins in Tabs. 2-3 and 8 potentially unfair. The paper does not clarify whether baselines were fine-tuned on the new dataset, which weakens the central comparative claims.

On established external benchmarks (RefCOCO, Ref-ZOM in Tab. 4), SAM3-I is not clearly dominant: UniPixel surpasses it on RefCOCO. The paper frames these as 'competitive or superior,' which overstates the evidence; results on ReasonSeg or other reasoning-segmentation benchmarks would strengthen the reasoning claims.

The one-to-many subset is small (2,941 samples, 7,449 masks) relative to the overall dataset, so the claimed advantage in this setting rests on limited data, and the dataset itself remains imbalanced (a bias the authors acknowledge but that also affects the conclusions drawn from Tab. 3).

Some methodological details are underspecified or confusing: the distinction between simple and complex instruction branches during inference, how the concept embeddings z^o used in the anchoring loss are obtained, whether the detector adapter is trained or frozen, and the exact role of MHSA in the cascaded adapter. The evaluation metric gIoU deviates from the standard oIoU convention on RefCOCO, complicating comparison with published numbers.

The paper claims 'we have released SAM3-I together with the HMPL-Instruct dataset,' but the code/dataset URL is a placeholder in the manuscript ('available at'), which hampers verifiability at review time.

Dataset construction relies on Qwen3-VL-8B both for generation and for verification (accepting instruction sets only at 100% inspector accuracy), which risks systematic MLLM-specific linguistic biases and self-agreement artifacts; no inter-annotator agreement statistics or human quality audits of the auto-generated portions are reported.

Novelty is moderate: adapter-based parameter-efficient tuning of SAM-family models and contrastive/ranking alignment losses are well-established techniques; the contribution lies primarily in their careful composition for the new PIS task and the dataset, rather than in fundamentally new methodology.

Minor clarity issues: occasional typos ('SAM-I' in Sec. 3, 'performs well to diverse benchmarks'), Eq. 5/6 notation (KL on 'mask distributions' vs. predicted masks needs clarification), and the '*' convention in Tab. 2 (concept scores retained by construction) could be misread as an empirical result of preservation.
